Article.ArticleTitle: Association between augmented renal clearance, antibiotic exposure and clinical outcome in critically ill septic patients receiving high doses of β-lactams administered by continuous infusion. a prospective observational study.

Abstract.AbstractText: This study aimed to assess whether augmented renal clearance (ARC) impacts negatively on antibiotic concentrations and clinical outcomes in patients treated by high doses of β-lactams administered continuously for a first infection in surgical intensive care unit.

Over a 9-month period, all critically ill patients treated by one of the monitored β-lactam antibiotics for a documented infection without renal impairment were eligible. During the first three days of antibiotic therapy, every patient underwent 24-hour creatinine clearance (CrCL) measurements and therapeutic drug monitoring. The main outcome was the rate of β-lactam under-dosing defined by a free drug concentration under 4 times the MIC of the known pathogen. The secondary outcomes were the rates of sub-exposure for β-lactam and therapeutic failure. The performance of CrCL in predicting the occurrence of β-lactam under-dosing was assessed by a receiver operating characteristic curve and the best threshold was assessed using multivariable logistic regression to determine whether ARC was an independent risk factor for sub-exposure and therapeutic failure.

Over the study period, 79 patients were included and 235 samples were analyzed. The rate of under-dosing<4xMIC was 12%, with a significant association with CrCL (p < 0.0001). A threshold of CrCL ≥ 170 ml/min had a sensitivity and specificity of 0.93 (95%CI: 0.77 - 0.99) and 0.65 (95%CI: 0.58 - 0.71) for predicting β-lactam under-dosing<4xMIC. Mean CrCL values ≥ 170ml/min over the first three days of antibiotic therapy were significantly associated with sub-exposure<4xMIC (OR = 10.1 [2.4 - 41.6], p = 0.001). Patients with sub-exposure<4xMIC presented higher rates of therapeutic failure (OR: 6.3 [1.2 - 33.2], p = 0.03).

Mean CrCL values ≥ 170 ml/min remain at risk of sub-exposure for β-lactam despite high doses of β-lactams administered continuously. Sub-exposure for β-lactam was associated with higher rates of therapeutic failure in septic critically ill patients.
